questions.stem: Daniel, 32, is sitting upright in ED after being bottled. The paramedic dressing has come off. A 5 cm wound over the right sternocleidomastoid oozes dark blood, and a sucking noise is heard at the wound with each breath in. He is talking in full sentences. What is your immediate action?
options: Probe the wound with a gloved finger to check whether platysma has been breached
Press directly on the wound, then apply an occlusive dressing and lay him flat in-line
Sit him further upright and cover the wound loosely with gauze to slow venous bleeding
Apply a cervical collar and take him straight to CT angiography of the neck
questions.why: A sucking neck wound means a cut vein is pulling in air. Occlude it straight away with pressure and an occlusive dressing, then lay him flat or head-down with in-line stabilisation. This raises venous pressure in the neck and stops air entrainment.
notes: Never probe a penetrating neck wound: it can dislodge clot, restart bleeding and let in more air, and it adds nothing to the decision to image or explore.
Sitting upright lowers venous pressure in the neck, which makes air entrainment and venous air embolism more likely, and a loose dressing does not seal the wound.
Imaging comes only after the wound is sealed and he is stable; sending him to CT with the wound open leaves the risk of air embolism untreated.

questions.stem: Daniel, 32, is stable after his neck wound was occluded. Both nostrils are blocked. Both sides of the septum show smooth, fluctuant, red-purple swellings that do not shrink with decongestant. CT shows displaced fractures of both nasal bones with soft tissue thickening on both sides of the septum. He wants to go home. What is the most appropriate plan for his nose?
options: Discharge with ENT clinic review in 5–7 days once the swelling has settled
Closed reduction of the nasal bones in ED now, before the swelling increases
Topical decongestant and saline spray, with GP review in 48 hours
Same-day drainage of both haematomas, packing, antibiotics; fracture review at 5–7 days
questions.why: A septal haematoma is an emergency and is drained the same day, then packed or splinted, with antibiotics. This prevents abscess, cartilage necrosis, perforation and saddle nose. Nasal bone fractures can wait for review in 5–7 days, once the swelling has settled.
notes: Waiting 5–7 days suits an isolated nasal fracture, but leaving a septal haematoma that long risks abscess and cartilage necrosis.
Reducing the fracture does not drain the haematoma, and swelling makes it hard to judge alignment early; the haematoma is the urgent problem.
A haematoma that does not shrink with decongestant is a collection of blood, not swollen mucosa, and needs drainage; sprays and delayed review miss it.

questions.stem: Daniel, 32, was punched in the nose. Both sides of his septum have smooth, fluctuant, red-purple swellings that do not shrink with decongestant. You explain that without drainage today the septal cartilage may die, leaving a perforation or a saddle nose. What is the main mechanism of the cartilage necrosis?
options: It compresses the anterior ethmoidal artery, infarcting the cartilage's own vessels
Bacterial enzymes from nasal flora digest the cartilage within the first few hours
Raised pressure in Kiesselbach's plexus causes venous thrombosis within the cartilage
It lifts the mucoperichondrium off avascular cartilage that relies on it for nutrients
questions.why: Septal cartilage has no blood vessels of its own. It gets its nutrients by diffusion from the overlying mucoperichondrium. A haematoma separates the two, so the cartilage becomes ischaemic and can die within days. A bilateral haematoma is the highest risk.
notes: The cartilage has no intrinsic vessels to infarct. The anterior ethmoidal artery supplies the mucosa, not vessels inside the cartilage.
Infection (septal abscess) is a later complication of an undrained haematoma. It is not the main early mechanism, and it does not happen within hours.
Kiesselbach's plexus is a mucosal plexus in Little's area. Thrombosis there does not explain necrosis of cartilage that has no blood vessels.

questions.stem: Daniel's CT angiogram shows that the right external jugular vein is cut beneath a glass wound over the sternocleidomastoid. Before the wound was occluded, a sucking noise was heard with each inspiration while he sat upright. Which anatomical feature best explains why the cut vein stayed open and drew in air?
options: It lies within the carotid sheath, splinted open by the common carotid artery
It has no valves along its course, so air passes freely towards the heart
It pierces the investing layer of deep cervical fascia, which binds its wall open
It lies deep to sternocleidomastoid, which tents the vein open with each breath
questions.why: The external jugular vein runs superficial to sternocleidomastoid, deep to platysma. Above the clavicle it pierces the investing layer of deep cervical fascia, and its wall is fixed to that fascia there. A cut vein therefore stays open instead of collapsing, and negative venous pressure during inspiration draws air in.
notes: The internal jugular vein lies in the carotid sheath. The external jugular vein is superficial, outside the sheath.
The external jugular vein does have valves, near its end and above the clavicle, though they are often incompetent; whether it has valves does not explain why the cut wall stays open.
The external jugular vein crosses superficial to sternocleidomastoid, which is why it is visible and why this wound reached it.
